rows.verified: Occupational asthma is an allergic reaction that can occur after exposure to respiratory sensitisers at work.
Examples of respiratory sensitisers include flour and wood dust.
Sensitisation can create a hypersensitive state in the airways.
After sensitisation, further exposure even at relatively low levels may trigger an asthma attack.
Symptoms can include wheezing, coughing, chest tightness and shortness of breath.
Workplace dusts can also cause rhinitis and eye irritation.
COSHH management includes assessing risk, preventing exposure where reasonably practicable and adequately controlling remaining exposure.
Dust monitoring, plant examination, training and suitable health surveillance can form part of control arrangements.
Risk depends on the sensitiser, airborne concentration, exposure route and duration, controls and individual susceptibility.
Occupational-asthma evidence is substance-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
Employers should assess and control workplace risks from bloodborne viruses using safe working practices and suitable controls.
Contaminated sharps can transmit hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.
Where sharps are required, employers should consider whether a safer sharp device can be used.
Sharps activities should be risk assessed to identify how an injury could occur.
Needles should not be bent or forced and should be kept pointing away from hands and the body during handling.
Used sharps should be disposed of immediately in an appropriate sharps container at the point of use.

rows.source: HSE safe working practices for BBVs
rows.verified: Workplaces must have arrangements for responding to potential bloodborne-virus exposure incidents.
Relevant incidents may be reportable under RIDDOR, and local records should capture incidents and underlying causes.
Transmission risk depends on the virus, source viral load, exposure type and site, and the volume of infected material transferred.
Bloodborne-virus evidence is incident- and exposure-specific and is not an exact parcel-level infection probability.
